source.title: Monosemanticity in Recommender Systems
source.authors: Yagel Alfasi; Eden Rzezak; Eadan Schechter

record.tranche_reason: The study extends monosemanticity analysis to collaborative-filtering recommender embeddings and reports semantic-coherence and intervention results in that new setting. It does not test the specific model, architectures, or explanation-evaluation procedures named in V1–V7.
record.gate_note: The study measures semantic coherence of MSAE latent features and intervenes on a selected feature subset, so those outcomes are recorded. SAE-versus-MSAE recommendation-ranking comparisons are not rows because they measure reconstruction fidelity, not the claim's named neuron properties. The paper's discussion of prior work is not treated as a result.
record.test_reason: The study does not test any version of the claim. It analyses latents of a sparse autoencoder trained on 20-dimensional matrix-factorization item embeddings. These are trained replacement features, not a network's own neurons. The setting is a recommender, not a language or vision model. It never audits native units: the MF embedding dimensions are asserted to be opaque but never measured. It builds no attribution graphs and runs no simulation scoring of explanations. It discusses superposition and monosemanticity only in general terms, framing monosemanticity as something induced by sparsity, and does not engage the essay's claim. The reader's T3 'tests' guess is not supported, because no result bears on what any version names.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is essentially right. One addition: the authors claim causal validation of a 'gender-sensitive axis'. They also explicitly note that their coherence score and LLM-label coherence diverge, as with N3, which gets a coherent label but a low score.
record.recipe_differences: This study trains a 50-feature Matryoshka sparse autoencoder on matrix-factorization item embeddings, scores item-set geometric coherence, generates labels from top-activating items, and intervenes on selected latent activations. It does not audit native language-model neuron poles or test explanations against held-out activating examples.
record.method_sensitivity: Intervention strength varies; reported response curve covers scaling factors 2–16. The study uses 50 sampled users for interventions and 5,000 items for the score analysis.

fits_no_version.finding: MSAE latents on Amazon Fashion MF item embeddings show a bimodal coherence score (0.075–0.201). LLM labels grow more specific with latent index. Scaling six selected 'women-associated' latents shifts the women share only from 0.53 to 0.54 (amplify) or 0.52 (suppress), with Overlap@50 at 0.97.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Matryoshka SAE latents trained on collaborative-filtering embeddings show a broad-to-specific semantic gradient, and selected latents give small directional control of recommendations.

record.problems: Evidence is limited to one domain and one dataset, with a 50-neuron dictionary. The intervention uses 50 sampled users. Semantic labels are generated by Claude Opus 4.5 without reported human validation. The authors state that their geometric-coherence metric does not directly measure human-perceived interpretability. No error bars or uncertainty estimates are reported for the relevant results.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant measured results were left out. The SAE-versus-MSAE recommendation-ranking metrics and list overlap in Section 5.1 were not included because they evaluate reconstruction and ranking fidelity rather than the neuron properties named by the claim.

untested.parts: No audit of Qwen3-32B neuron poles or of shares with one, two or unknown jobs.
No language models, dense or MoE, and no scale comparison. Native units are never examined.
No InceptionV1, cat-and-car neuron, pose or recursive generalization.
No test of architecture, regularization or tooling as causes of messy neurons. No estimates of the interpretable-neuron share.
No attribution graphs built from native neurons, and no comparison with replacement-model reconstruction error.
Explanations from activating examples are not checked against held-out activations.
No simulation-based scoring of explanations on new inputs.

record.verdict_notes: The study treats raw MF embeddings as opaque and does not measure them. Every interpretability result concerns SAE latents, so neither the claim's native-neuron framing nor its challenges are tested. The intervention effects are very small (±1 point) on 50 users, with no uncertainty reported. Labels come from Claude Opus 4.5 without human validation.

versions.untested_parts: Does not audit Qwen3-32B or report the claimed shares of one-job, two-related-job, or not-understood neuron poles.
Studies one recommender-system dataset and does not test language models, dense versus mixture-of-experts models, or scaling to large parameter counts.
Does not examine InceptionV1 or the cat-and-car example, pose detection, or recursive generalization.
Does not test the proposed causes of messy late-layer neurons or estimate interpretable-neuron shares for vision models.
Does not build attribution graphs or evaluate whether they reconstruct behavior without a replacement model.
Does not test whether explanations based on activating examples predict activation on held-out examples.
Does not simulate neuron explanations on new text or report the share of explanations receiving good automated scores.

rows.subject: Matryoshka Sparse Autoencoder (MSAE) on Amazon Fashion MF item embeddings
rows.operation_detail: Computed the adapted Monosemanticity Score (activation-weighted pairwise cosine similarity of activating items in MF embedding space) for 50 neurons using 5,000 items.
rows.value: Scores range from approximately 0.075 to 0.201; distribution described as bimodal, with one cluster at 0.08–0.11 and another at 0.16–0.19.
rows.note: The paper says the score measures geometric coherence, not semantic-label interpretability.
rows.check: The score is on SAE latents, not native neurons. The authors say it measures geometric coherence, not interpretability, so it cannot speak to the one-job shares in V1/V2.

rows.subject: Matryoshka Sparse Autoencoder (MSAE) on Amazon Fashion MF item embeddings
rows.operation_detail: Reported the adapted Monosemanticity Score for neuron N3 and its LLM-generated label.
rows.value: MS 0.076; labeled with a women’s apparel concept, despite the paper describing its activating items as geometrically dispersed.
rows.note: The authors treat geometric coherence and label coherence as distinct notions.

rows.subject: Matryoshka Sparse Autoencoder (MSAE) on Amazon Fashion MF item embeddings
rows.operation_detail: Qualitatively grouped LLM-generated labels by neuron-index range.
rows.value: Labels described as broad, such as “Clothing, Shoes & Jewelry,” with no consistent subcategory specialization.
rows.note: Qualitative description of generated labels, not an independently validated count of single-job features.

rows.subject: Matryoshka Sparse Autoencoder (MSAE) on Amazon Fashion MF embeddings
rows.operation_detail: Selected neurons based on LLM-generated labels and inspected their top-activating items.
rows.value: 6 of 50 neurons (approximately 12%) were selected as associated with women-oriented product categories; top-activating items were described as consistently including women’s apparel and accessories.
rows.note: Selection was based on automated labels and inspection; the study does not report an independent human validation.
rows.check: This is a selection step: 6 of 50 SAE latents were chosen from LLM labels for the intervention. It is not a measured result. The 12% is the size of the selected set, not a share of interpretable units.
